reason: The differentiation signals identify the stem-cell subset that develops into muscle precursors, a necessary first step toward a muscle fibre.
expectation: The selected cells will develop toward muscle precursors.

effect: The signals produced myoblasts that make muscle and fusion proteins, so the next step is to join them.
reaction: The contrast with fibroblasts exporting collagen is useful.
reason: The fusion proteins match the membranes of adjacent myoblasts and should join the precursor cells.
expectation: The myoblasts will fuse into a multinucleated muscle fibre.

effect: Fusion produced a multinucleated fibre with actin–myosin machinery, but its grip sites are still covered.
reaction: The distinction between one fibre and its many nuclei is clear.
reason: The calcium pulse reaches the filaments and should enable them to interact.
expectation: Calcium will uncover actin's grip sites so the fibre can pull.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites, allowing myosin to pull the filaments past each other; the fibre now needs to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between filament sliding and filament shortening is useful.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes should return calcium to storage, ending the signal.
expectation: Calcium will be pumped back into storage so the fibre can relax and become ready again.

effect: ATP-powered calcium pumps restored the fibre to a relaxed, ready state, and the goal now is to build and attach both muscles.
reaction: It is useful that relaxation also requires ATP and an outside pull to lengthen the fibre.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty muscle-head spaces that the developed fibres could fill.
expectation: The fibres will be organized into a biceps muscle with tendons.

alternatives.reason: The triceps sheaths also need fibres, but either muscle seems a reasonable place to start.

effect: The fibres first needed extracellular matrix to form fascicles; enough bundles are now available for both muscles.
reaction: The connective layers clarify how individual fibres are grouped, though I had missed that intermediate step.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty head spaces that the muscle fascicles can fill.
expectation: The fascicles will form a biceps muscle within its sheaths and tendons.

alternatives.reason: The fascicles could instead be used to build the triceps first.

effect: The fascicles formed the two biceps heads, with connective tissue transmitting force to the tendons.
reaction: The force-transmission inset makes the tendons' role clearer.
reason: The remaining fascicles can fill the triceps sheaths to build the second muscle.
expectation: The fascicles will form a triceps with its tendons.

effect: The remaining fascicles formed the triceps, so both muscles are ready to be attached to the skeleton.
reaction: The cutaway distinguishes the three heads and their different attachment routes.
reason: The biceps tendons lead toward the shoulder and radius, so attaching them to the arm skeleton is a clear next step.
expectation: The biceps will attach across the elbow to the arm skeleton.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs attachment, and could plausibly be attached first.

effect: The biceps is attached across the elbow and flexes it; the assembly still needs an extensor.
reaction: The two poses clarify how the biceps pulls on the radius.
reason: The triceps is the remaining muscle and fits the empty extensor slot.
expectation: The triceps will attach across the elbow and provide extension opposite the biceps.

effect: The triceps filled the extensor slot, completing the arm assembly and showing how its attachment produces extension opposite the biceps.
reaction: The paired poses make the opposing movements clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following calcium-triggered filament sliding through relaxation was worthwhile: the planned images distinguish sliding from filament shortening and show why relaxation also needs ATP.

leastWorthwhile.text: Filling the two sets of sheaths was comparatively repetitive, although the different head counts and attachment routes added anatomical context.

surprise.text: I had expected to put fibres directly into a muscle sheath; the compatibility feedback revealed that extracellular matrix first organizes them into fascicles.

arbitrary.text: The need for fascicles was not clear to me before the attempted sheath combination, though the resulting connective layers gave that intermediate a purpose.

continue.text: Yes, I would choose to continue: connecting filament-level pulling to tendon attachments and opposing elbow movements made the construction informative, even if some assembly steps were predictable.
